learn: A community is a place where people live, work and play.
A city is a big, busy community with tall buildings. A town is smaller.
A rural community is in the countryside, with farms and lots of open land.
check: A community in the countryside with farms is...
Which community has tall buildings and many people?
What do people do in a community?
lessons.try: Decide if you live in a city, a town or a rural community.

learn: Communities have places that help people.
A library lends books. A hospital helps sick people. A fire station holds fire trucks.
Parks give people space to play and rest.
check: Where do sick people get help?
lessons.try: Name three places in your community you have visited.

learn: People in communities work together to solve problems.
Neighbours may clean a park, help an older person or share food.
Volunteers help without being paid.
check: Do people in communities work together?
lessons.try: Think of one way your class could help your community.

learn: A community is a place where people live, work and play together.
Your neighborhood, town and school are communities.
People in a community help each other.
check: A community is where people live, work and...
lessons.try: Name three communities you belong to.

learn: An urban community is a city. It has many people and tall buildings.
Cities have busy streets, buses, apartments and many stores.
Phoenix and Tucson are cities in Arizona.
check: Which is a city in Arizona?
lessons.try: Draw a city street with buildings and buses.

learn: A suburban community is near a city. It has houses with yards.
People often drive to the city for work.
Suburbs have schools, parks and shopping centers.
lessons.try: Draw a suburban street with houses and yards.

learn: A rural community is in the countryside, with farms and lots of open land.
Homes are far apart.
Farmers in rural areas grow food for cities.
check: A rural community has lots of...
lessons.try: Draw a rural place with a farm.

learn: Urban, suburban and rural communities are different but all have people who need each other.
Cities are crowded. Rural areas are spread out. Suburbs are in between.
Every community has homes, jobs and helpers.
check: Which is spread out with farms?
lessons.try: Make a chart comparing city, suburb and countryside.

learn: Communities have important places: school, library, hospital, fire station, park, grocery store.
Each place meets a need.
The hospital helps sick people. The library lends books.
check: Where do sick people get help?
Each place in a community meets a...
lessons.try: Make a list of five places in your community and what they do.

learn: People in communities travel by car, bus, bike, train and walking.
Roads, sidewalks and bike lanes help people get around.
Some cities have light rail or subways.
lessons.try: List the ways your family travels around town.

learn: Neighbors are people who live near you.
Good neighbors say hello, help each other and keep things tidy.
You can be a good neighbor too.
lessons.try: Do something kind for a neighbor with a grown-up.

learn: People in a community work together to solve problems.
They clean parks, build playgrounds and help after storms.
Many hands make light work.
lessons.try: Help clean one shared space with your family.

learn: Communities have events: fairs, parades, farmers markets and festivals.
Events bring people together to have fun and share.
Many towns have a yearly celebration.
lessons.try: Find out about one event in your community.

learn: A school is a community with students, teachers, the principal and staff.
Everyone has a job: learning, teaching, cooking, cleaning, keeping us safe.
We all help make school a good place.
check: Everyone in a school has a...
lessons.try: Thank a school worker you see every day.

learn: Communities can be urban, suburban or rural.
They have places, helpers and events.
People in communities work together.
lessons.try: Draw a map of your community with five important places.

learn: Rules are for a group, like a class or a family.
Laws are rules for everyone in a community, state or country.
Laws keep people safe and help things be fair.
check: To keep people safe and be fair
lessons.try: Name one law you know, like stopping at a red light.

learn: Speed limits tell drivers how fast they can go.
Seat belt laws keep people safe in cars.
Littering laws keep parks and streets clean.
check: What keeps people safe in cars?
lessons.try: Look for a traffic sign on your next walk or ride.

learn: Without rules, people could get hurt or be treated unfairly.
When we follow rules, everyone gets a fair turn.
If a rule is not fair, people can work together to change it peacefully.
check: How can people change an unfair rule?
lessons.try: Imagine a game with no rules. What would happen?

learn: Rules are made by families, schools and groups.
Laws are rules made by governments for everyone.
Breaking a law has bigger consequences.
lessons.try: Name one rule at home and one law in your town.

learn: Traffic laws keep drivers, riders and walkers safe.
Stop at red lights. Use crosswalks. Wear seatbelts.
Speed limits tell how fast cars may go.
check: At a red light, drivers must...
Speed limits tell how ___ cars may go.
lessons.try: Find a crosswalk and a stop sign on a walk.

learn: Some laws protect our safety: children ride in car seats, swimmers follow pool rules.
Fire codes make buildings safe.
Safety laws protect people from getting hurt.
lessons.try: Check that your car seat or seatbelt is buckled correctly.

learn: Property is something that belongs to someone.
Laws say we cannot take or damage other people's property.
Public property, like parks, belongs to everyone.
lessons.try: Name something that is your property and something that is public property.

learn: Some laws protect animals, plants, water and air.
You may not pick flowers in national parks or hunt some animals.
Littering is against the law.
check: In national parks, picking flowers is often...
lessons.try: Find out one rule at a park near you.

learn: In towns, the city council makes laws.
In states, lawmakers called the legislature make laws.
For the country, Congress makes laws.
check: Who makes laws for the whole country?
Who makes laws for a town?
lessons.try: Find out the name of your city or town council.

learn: Police officers make sure people follow laws.
Judges decide what happens when laws are broken.
Courts are where judges work.
check: Who makes sure people follow laws?
Who decides what happens when a law is broken?
lessons.try: Draw a judge in a courtroom.

learn: A consequence is what happens after a choice.
Good choices can bring good consequences. Breaking rules brings consequences like losing a privilege.
Consequences help people learn.
check: A consequence is what happens after a...
Breaking rules can mean losing a...
lessons.try: Think of a good choice you made and its consequence.

learn: Good rules are fair, clear and make sense.
A fair rule applies to everyone the same way.
If a rule is unfair, people can work to change it peacefully.
check: If a rule is unfair, people can ___ to change it.
lessons.try: Write a fair rule for a game.

learn: Games and sports have rules so everyone plays fairly.
Referees and umpires make sure rules are followed.
Without rules, games would not work.
check: Rules in sports help everyone play...
Who makes sure sports rules are followed?
lessons.try: Explain the rules of your favorite game to someone.

learn: A constitution is a written set of rules for a group.
The United States Constitution is our country's main set of laws.
A class can write its own constitution and everyone signs it.
check: A constitution is a written set of...
Our country's main laws are in the...
lessons.try: Write three rules for your family constitution. Have everyone sign.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Rules and Laws
learn: Rules are made by groups. Laws are made by governments.
Laws keep us safe, protect property and nature.
Police enforce laws, judges decide consequences.
lessons.try: Make a poster showing three laws that keep you safe.

learn: A leader is someone who helps guide a group.
A principal leads a school. A coach leads a team.
Good leaders listen, are fair and help others.
lessons.try: Name a leader in your school.

learn: A mayor leads a city or town.
A governor leads a state.
The president leads the United States.
lessons.try: Find out the name of your town's mayor with a grown-up.

learn: In the United States, people choose many leaders by voting.
Each vote counts the same. The choice with the most votes wins.
Your class can vote too, like choosing a class pet name.
check: How do people choose many leaders?
The one with the most votes
Does each vote count the same?
lessons.try: Hold a vote at home about what to have for dinner.

learn: Leaders guide groups, make plans and help solve problems.
Good leaders listen and are fair.
Leaders work for the good of the group.
check: Leaders work for the good of the...
lessons.try: Describe a leader you know and what they do.

learn: Parents lead families. Teachers lead classes. The principal leads the school.
Coaches lead teams.
Even students can be class leaders.
lessons.try: Name a leader at home, at school and on a team.

learn: The mayor is the leader of a city or town.
The mayor helps make plans for roads, parks and safety.
People vote to choose the mayor.
check: The mayor plans for roads and...
lessons.try: Find out the name of your town's mayor.

learn: The governor is the leader of a state.
Arizona has a governor who works at the state capitol in Phoenix.
The governor signs state laws.
lessons.try: Find Phoenix, the capital of Arizona, on a map.

learn: The president is the leader of the United States.
The president lives and works in the White House.
Americans vote for a president every four years.
lessons.try: Learn the name of the current president.

learn: Good leaders are honest, fair, responsible and kind.
They make good decisions and keep promises.
They help everyone, not just friends.
lessons.try: Make a list of qualities you think a good leader has.

learn: Voting is how people choose leaders and make decisions.
Each person gets one vote. The choice with the most votes wins.
In the United States, adults 18 and older can vote.
check: The choice with the most votes...
In the U.S., people can vote at age...
lessons.try: Have a family vote on a weekend activity.

learn: When adults vote, they use a secret ballot.
No one has to share how they voted.
Secret ballots keep voting fair.
check: Does a voter have to share how they voted?
lessons.try: Have a class or family secret ballot vote with paper slips.

learn: You can lead by setting a good example.
Help a classmate, start a cleanup, or lead a game fairly.
Leaders listen to others' ideas.
check: You can lead by setting a good...
A good leader of a game makes sure everyone gets a...
lessons.try: Lead a game with friends and make sure everyone gets a turn.

learn: Many leaders changed our country: George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, Harriet Tubman, Martin Luther King Jr.
Harriet Tubman led people to freedom on the Underground Railroad.
Leaders can be brave, even in hard times.
lessons.try: Learn one fact about a leader from history.

learn: Native American nations have their own leaders and governments.
Arizona is home to many nations, including the Navajo Nation, the Hopi Tribe and the Tohono O'odham Nation.
Tribal leaders make decisions for their people.
check: Native American nations have their own...
Tribal leaders make decisions for their...
lessons.try: Find the Navajo Nation on a map of Arizona.

learn: Leaders guide groups at home, at school and in government.
Mayors lead towns, governors lead states and the president leads the country.
People choose leaders by voting.
lessons.try: Write what you would do if you were mayor for a day.

learn: Maps have a title that tells what the map shows.
A map key or legend explains the symbols.
A compass rose shows the directions north, south, east and west.
check: What shows directions on a map?
lessons.try: Look at a map and find the title, key and compass rose.

learn: The four main directions are north, south, east and west.
On most maps, north is at the top and south is at the bottom.
East is on the right and west is on the left. Remember: Never Eat Soggy Waffles.
check: On most maps, north is at the...
lessons.try: Point north, south, east and west in your room.

learn: You can make a map of your school, house or neighbourhood.
Use symbols and make a key so others can read your map.
Add a compass rose so people know the directions.
check: What should your map have so others can read it?
What tells people the directions on your map?
lessons.try: Make a map of your street or block with a key.

learn: A map's title tells what the map shows.
The key, or legend, explains the symbols.
Always read the title and key first.
check: A map's title tells what the map...
Another word for map key is...
lessons.try: Find the title and key on a map of a zoo or park.

learn: Map symbols are small pictures that stand for real things.
A tree symbol for a park, a cross for a hospital, a book for a library.
Symbols save space on maps.
check: A book symbol might mean a...
lessons.try: Make symbols for your school, home and a park.

learn: North, south, east and west are cardinal directions.
A compass rose shows them. N is usually at the top.
Never Eat Soggy Waffles helps you remember N, E, S, W going clockwise.
check: N on a compass rose is usually at the...
Never Eat Soggy Waffles helps remember...
lessons.try: Label N, E, S and W on the walls of your room.

learn: A compass has a needle that always points north.
Once you know north, you can find the other directions.
Hikers and sailors use compasses.
check: If you face north, east is on your...
lessons.try: Use a compass (or a phone compass) to find north at home.

learn: Use directions to move on a map: go north two blocks, then east one block.
Trace the path with your finger.
Check the compass rose as you go.
check: To move on a map we use...
If you go north then south the same amount, you end up...
lessons.try: Give someone directions on a map to a treasure.

learn: Some maps have a grid of squares with letters and numbers.
A place might be in square B3.
Find the letter, then the number.
check: To find B3, find B then...
lessons.try: Make a grid map of your room. Tell what is in A1.

learn: A map is smaller than the real place.
A scale tells how much smaller: one inch might equal one mile.
Scales help us know how far things are.
check: A map is ___ than the real place.
A scale tells how far things...
lessons.try: Use a map scale to find how far your school is from a park.

learn: A neighborhood map shows streets, houses, parks and stores.
Street names help you find your way.
Your address is on a street.
lessons.try: Draw a map of your street with your home and two neighbors.

learn: A map of Arizona shows cities, rivers, mountains and deserts.
The Grand Canyon is in the north. Tucson is in the south.
The Colorado River runs along the western border.
check: The Grand Canyon is in the ___ of Arizona.
Tucson is in the ___ of Arizona.
The Colorado River runs along the ___ border.
lessons.try: Find Phoenix, Tucson and the Grand Canyon on a map of Arizona.

learn: The United States has 50 states.
Arizona is in the Southwest. Its neighbors include California, Nevada, Utah, New Mexico and Mexico.
Alaska and Hawaii are far from the other states.
check: Which state is an island chain?
lessons.try: Color Arizona and its neighbors on a U.S. map.

learn: Road maps show roads. Weather maps show weather. Physical maps show land and water.
Each map is made for a purpose.
Choose the right map for the job.
check: Each map is made for a...
lessons.try: Find three kinds of maps in books or online.

learn: Maps have titles, keys, symbols, compass roses, grids and scales.
We use directions to move on maps.
There are maps of neighborhoods, states and countries.
lessons.try: Make a map of your school with all the map parts.

learn: Landforms are shapes of land.
A mountain is very high land. A hill is lower. A valley is low land between hills.
A plain is wide, flat land. An island is land with water all around it.
check: Land with water all around it is...
lessons.try: Make a landform out of clay or play dough.

learn: Oceans are huge bodies of salt water.
Lakes have land all around them. Rivers flow across land to a lake or an ocean.
Most of Earth is covered by water.
check: Is most of Earth covered by water?
lessons.try: Find an ocean, a lake and a river on a map.

learn: Earth has seven continents: North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia and Antarctica.
Earth has five oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic and Southern.
The United States is on the continent of North America.
lessons.try: Point to North America and the Pacific Ocean on a globe or world map.

learn: Mountains are very high land with steep sides.
The tallest mountain in Arizona is Humphreys Peak near Flagstaff.
Mountains can have snow on top even when it is warm below.
lessons.try: Build a mountain out of clay or sand.

learn: Hills are raised land, smaller than mountains.
Valleys are low land between hills or mountains.
Rivers often flow through valleys.
check: A valley is ___ land between hills.
lessons.try: Shape hills and a valley with a blanket.

learn: Plains are wide, flat lands. Many farms are on plains.
A plateau is high, flat land with steep sides.
Much of northern Arizona is the Colorado Plateau.
check: Northern Arizona is on the Colorado...
lessons.try: Find a picture of a plain and a plateau. Compare them.

learn: A desert is a dry place with little rain.
Deserts can be hot or cold.
The Sonoran Desert in Arizona has saguaro cacti found nowhere else in the U.S.
lessons.try: Draw the Sonoran Desert with saguaros.

learn: A canyon is a deep valley with steep sides, often cut by a river.
The Grand Canyon was carved by the Colorado River over millions of years.
It is one of the seven natural wonders of the world.
check: A canyon is a deep valley with ___ sides.
The Grand Canyon was carved by the...
The Grand Canyon took ___ to carve.
lessons.try: Look at pictures of the Grand Canyon. Count the rock layers.

learn: An island is land with water all around it.
A peninsula is land with water on three sides.
Hawaii is islands. Florida is a peninsula.
check: A peninsula has water on ___ sides.
lessons.try: Make an island and a peninsula in a tray with sand and water.

learn: Oceans are huge bodies of salt water.
There are five oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic and Southern.
Oceans cover most of Earth.
lessons.try: Find all five oceans on a globe.

learn: A river is fresh water that flows across land.
Rivers start in high places and flow downhill to lakes or oceans.
The Colorado, Gila and Salt Rivers are in Arizona.
lessons.try: Pour water on a sand hill and watch it make a river.

learn: A lake is a body of water with land all around.
A pond is a small lake.
Lake Powell and Lake Havasu are in Arizona and were made by dams.
check: Lake Havasu was made by a...
lessons.try: Find Lake Powell on a map.

learn: Earth has seven continents: North America, South America, Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia and Antarctica.
Asia is the biggest. Australia is the smallest.
Antarctica is covered in ice.
check: Which continent is covered in ice?
lessons.try: Point to all seven continents on a globe.

learn: People live differently based on land and water.
People near oceans may fish. People on plains may farm. People in deserts save water.
Landforms shape homes, food and jobs.
check: People in deserts need to save...
lessons.try: Think about how land near you affects your life.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Land and Water
learn: Landforms include mountains, hills, valleys, plains, plateaus, deserts, canyons, islands and peninsulas.
Bodies of water include oceans, rivers, lakes and ponds.
Earth has seven continents and five oceans.
check: Land with water all around is an...
lessons.try: Make a landform and water poster with labels.

learn: The past is what already happened. The present is now. The future is what will happen.
Words like yesterday, long ago and last year tell about the past.
Words like tomorrow and next year tell about the future.
lessons.try: Use "yesterday", "today" and "tomorrow" in sentences.

learn: A timeline shows events in the order they happened.
Older events go on the left. Newer events go on the right.
You can make a timeline of your own life.
check: Where do older events go on a timeline?
Can you make a timeline of your own life?
lessons.try: Make a timeline with three events from your life.

learn: Things change over time. Schools, toys and transportation are different from long ago.
Long ago, children wrote on small chalkboards called slates. Now we use paper and computers.
Some things stay the same: children still learn, play and help at home.
check: What did children write on long ago?
Do some things stay the same over time?
Transportation long ago and today is...
lessons.try: Ask an older person how school was different when they were young.

learn: Yesterday was the day before today. Tomorrow is the day after today.
Today is now, the present.
These words help us talk about time.
lessons.try: Tell what you did yesterday, what you are doing today and what you will do tomorrow.

learn: There are seven days: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday.
School days are usually Monday to Friday.
Saturday and Sunday are the weekend.
check: How many days in a week?
lessons.try: Sing or say the days of the week in order.

learn: There are 12 months: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November and December.
Each month has about 30 days.
Your birthday is in one month.
check: How many months are in a year?
lessons.try: Find your birthday month on a calendar.

learn: The past is time that has already happened.
When you were a baby is your past. Long ago is the past of our country.
We learn about the past from photos, stories and objects.
check: We learn about the past from...
When you were a baby is your...
lessons.try: Find an old photo of your family and talk about it.

learn: The future is time that has not happened yet.
Tomorrow, next year and when you grow up are the future.
We can plan and hope for the future.
lessons.try: Draw what you want to be in the future.

learn: A timeline shows events in order.
Your timeline might show: born, first steps, first word, started school.
Earlier events go on the left.
check: Which is the first event in your life?
lessons.try: Make a timeline of your life with five events.

learn: History timelines show events from long ago to now.
1776: our country began. 1969: people walked on the moon.
The bigger the number, the more recent the year.
check: People walked on the moon in...
lessons.try: Make a timeline with three events from history.

learn: A primary source is something from the time we are learning about.
Old letters, photos, tools and diaries are primary sources.
They help us see the past with our own eyes.
lessons.try: Look at an old object in your home. What does it tell you?

learn: Towns change over time.
A field may become a neighborhood. Old buildings may become new stores.
Old photos show how a town used to look.
check: Old photos show how a town...
lessons.try: Ask a grown-up what has changed in your town.

learn: Technology means tools people make.
Long ago, people wrote with quills. Today we type on computers.
Phones, cars and lights have changed a lot.
lessons.try: Draw an old tool and the new tool that does the same job.

learn: Some things do not change: families love each other, children play, people need food.
Holidays and traditions may stay for many years.
Change and sameness are both part of history.
lessons.try: Name two things that are the same now as long ago.

learn: Past, present and future describe time.
Calendars and timelines show order.
Primary sources teach us about the past.
lessons.try: Make a past, present and future poster about yourself.

learn: Long ago, many families lived in small houses, cabins or farmhouses.
Homes were heated by fireplaces and wood stoves.
Water often came from a well or a pump, not a tap.
check: How were homes heated long ago?
Where did water often come from?
lessons.try: Draw a home from long ago and a home today.

learn: Families long ago grew much of their own food.
Children helped by fetching water, feeding animals and gathering eggs.
Clothes were washed by hand on a washboard.
check: What did children do long ago?
lessons.try: Name one chore you do and one chore children did long ago.

learn: Children played games like tag, hopscotch, marbles and jump rope.
Families told stories, sang songs and played music together.
Many of these games are still played today.
check: Which game was played long ago?
Are some old games still played?
lessons.try: Play a game of hopscotch or tag from long ago.

learn: Pioneers were families who moved west long ago to build new homes.
They traveled in covered wagons pulled by oxen or horses.
The trip took months.
lessons.try: Draw a covered wagon.

learn: Pioneers built log cabins or sod houses from the land around them.
A fireplace was used for cooking and heat.
Homes often had one room for the whole family.
check: A fireplace was used for cooking and...
lessons.try: Build a log cabin with craft sticks.

learn: Children long ago had many chores.
They carried water, fed animals, gathered eggs and helped plant crops.
Work started early in the morning.
lessons.try: Compare your chores with a pioneer child's chores.

learn: Many children walked far to a one-room school.
They wrote on slates and read from McGuffey Readers.
Older children helped younger ones.
check: In one-room schools, older children helped...
lessons.try: Write on a small chalkboard like a slate.

learn: Families made their own clothes by spinning, weaving and sewing.
Children had few clothes and wore them until they wore out.
Clothes were passed down to younger brothers and sisters.
lessons.try: Try sewing a button with a grown-up.

learn: Families grew vegetables, raised animals and hunted.
They dried, salted and canned food to keep it for winter.
Bread was baked at home.
check: Families kept food for winter by...
lessons.try: Help bake bread or another food from scratch.

learn: Children played tag, hopscotch, jump rope and marbles.
Toys were often handmade: corn husk dolls, wooden tops, rag balls.
Children used imagination to play.
check: Which game was played long ago?
lessons.try: Make a simple toy like a corn husk or yarn doll.

learn: Native American families lived across the land long before pioneers came.
The Hopi built pueblos and grew corn. The Navajo built hogans and raised sheep.
Each nation had its own language, homes and traditions.
lessons.try: Draw a pueblo and a hogan.

learn: People traveled by horse, wagon, boat and foot.
The Pony Express carried mail by horse across the country.
Later, trains made travel faster.
check: The Pony Express carried mail by...
lessons.try: Write a letter as if it would be carried by the Pony Express.

learn: Compare: Then, water came from wells. Now, it comes from faucets.
Then, light came from candles. Now, from electric lights.
Some things are easier now, but families still work together.
lessons.try: Make a then-and-now chart with four rows.

learn: Elders can share what life was like when they were young.
Prepare questions: What games did you play? What was school like?
Listen carefully and write down answers.
check: Elders can share what life was ___ .
lessons.try: Interview an elder and share three things you learned.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Families Long Ago
learn: Long ago, families worked hard to grow food, make clothes and build homes.
Children had chores, went to one-room schools and played simple games.
Some things have changed, and some stay the same.
lessons.try: Make a book: A Day in the Life of a Child Long Ago.

learn: Goods are things people make or grow that we can buy.
Apples, shoes and books are goods.
Producers make goods. Consumers buy and use them.
lessons.try: Name three goods in your kitchen.

learn: A service is work someone does for others.
A haircut, a bus ride and a doctor's check-up are services.
Teachers, nurses and mail carriers provide services.
check: Is a bus ride a good or a service?
lessons.try: Name a service your family uses.

learn: Long ago, people traded goods instead of using money. This is called barter.
A farmer might trade eggs for shoes.
Today we mostly use money, but you can still trade things with friends.
check: A farmer might trade eggs for...
What do we mostly use today?
lessons.try: Trade a sticker or a pencil with a family member.

learn: Goods are things people make or grow that can be bought and sold.
Apples, shoes, books and toys are goods.
You can touch goods.
lessons.try: Find five goods in your kitchen.

learn: Services are work people do for others.
A haircut, a bus ride and teaching are services.
You cannot hold a service, but you can see it happen.
lessons.try: List three services your family used this week.

learn: Producers make goods or provide services.
A farmer produces corn. A baker produces bread. A doctor provides care.
Producers work to earn money.
lessons.try: Name three producers in your community.

learn: Consumers buy and use goods and services.
When you buy a snack, you are a consumer.
Everyone is a consumer.
check: Buying a snack makes you a...
lessons.try: Tell about the last thing you bought or used.

learn: Food goes on a journey: grown on a farm, trucked to a store, bought by a family.
Many workers help along the way.
Each step is a good or a service.
check: Food is first grown on a...
lessons.try: Draw the journey of a carton of milk.

learn: Factories are buildings where goods are made in large amounts.
Workers and machines make cars, clothes and toys.
An assembly line passes things from worker to worker.
check: An assembly line passes things from worker to...
Which is made in a factory?
lessons.try: Make a mini assembly line to build paper airplanes with family.

learn: Trading means swapping one thing for another without money.
Long ago, people traded goods like furs for tools.
Children trade cards or snacks.
check: Long ago people traded furs for...
lessons.try: Trade a toy with a sibling or friend (with permission).

learn: Scarcity means there is not enough of something for everyone who wants it.
When something is scarce, people must make choices.
Water is scarce in the desert, so people save it.
lessons.try: Talk about something that is scarce in your home.

learn: People work at many jobs: teacher, nurse, builder, chef, mechanic, farmer.
Some jobs make goods, some provide services.
Every job helps the community.
lessons.try: Ask a family member about their job.

learn: Workers use tools to do their jobs.
A chef uses pots. A builder uses a hammer. A farmer uses a tractor.
Tools help people work faster and better.
lessons.try: Match tools to jobs.

lessons.t: Needs Met by Goods and Services
learn: Goods and services meet our needs and wants.
A home is a need. A plumber's service keeps water running.
A toy is a want.
lessons.try: Sort goods and services into needs and wants.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Goods and Services
learn: Goods can be touched. Services are work done for others.
Producers make them, consumers buy them.
Scarcity means making choices.
lessons.try: Make a poster of a store that sells goods and offers a service.

learn: A penny is worth 1 cent. A nickel is worth 5 cents.
A dime is worth 10 cents, even though it is small. A quarter is worth 25 cents.
One hundred cents make one dollar.
check: How many cents make a dollar?
lessons.try: Sort real or play coins by their names.

learn: People earn money by working.
They spend money on needs first, like food and housing.
If there is money left, they may buy wants.
lessons.try: Make a list of needs and wants for a pretend shopping trip.

learn: Saving means keeping money to use later.
A bank keeps money safe. A piggy bank is a small home bank.
When you choose one thing, you give up another. Choosing wisely is important.
check: When you choose one thing you...
lessons.try: Pretend you have 10 dollars. Will you spend it all or save some?

learn: A penny is worth 1 cent. A nickel is worth 5 cents.
Lincoln is on the penny. Jefferson is on the nickel.
A nickel is bigger than a penny but worth more because of its value, not its size.
lessons.try: Sort pennies and nickels and count each.

learn: A dime is worth 10 cents. It is the smallest coin but worth more than a nickel.
A quarter is worth 25 cents. Washington is on the quarter.
Four quarters make a dollar.
check: How many quarters make a dollar?
lessons.try: Count dimes by tens and quarters by twenty-fives.

learn: Count coins starting with the biggest value.
A quarter, a dime and a penny: 25, 35, 36 cents.
Skip count by each coin's value.
check: A quarter and a dime is...
Two dimes and a nickel is...
lessons.try: Count a pile of mixed coins.

learn: A dollar is worth 100 cents.
It is a paper bill, also called a dollar bill.
Washington is on the one-dollar bill.
check: Who is on the one-dollar bill?
lessons.try: Show 100 cents in coins. Compare to a dollar bill.

learn: People earn money by working at jobs.
Children may earn by doing extra chores or selling lemonade.
Earning takes effort and time.
lessons.try: Talk about a way kids can earn money.

learn: Spending means using money to buy goods and services.
Think before you spend: Do I need it? Do I want it a lot?
Once money is spent, it is gone.
check: Before spending, ask: Do I ___ it?
Once money is spent, it is...
lessons.try: Pretend to shop with 50 cents. What will you buy?

learn: Saving means keeping money for later.
Save in a piggy bank or a bank account.
Saving helps you buy something big later or be ready for surprises.
lessons.try: Make a savings goal chart for something you want.

learn: A bank is a business that keeps people's money safe.
People deposit money (put it in) and withdraw money (take it out).
Banks may pay a little extra, called interest, for saving.
check: Putting money in a bank is a...
Extra money a bank pays for saving is...
lessons.try: Visit a bank or look at a bank's website with a grown-up.

learn: When you choose one thing, you give up another.
If you buy a ball, you cannot buy the book with the same money.
What you give up is called the opportunity cost.
check: When you choose one thing you give up...
What you give up is the...
Can you buy two things with money for one?
lessons.try: Choose between two treats. Tell what you gave up.

learn: A budget is a plan for money.
Decide how much to save, spend and share.
Many people use save, spend and share jars.
check: A budget is a plan for...
Three jars can be save, spend and...
lessons.try: Make three jars: save, spend and share.

learn: Sharing money helps people in need.
People give to food banks, shelters and charities.
Giving makes communities stronger.
check: A food bank gives food to...
lessons.try: Choose a charity and save coins to give.

learn: You know pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters and dollars.
People earn, spend, save and share money.
Every choice has an opportunity cost.
check: What you give up when choosing is...
lessons.try: Count coins to 50 cents and decide how to save, spend and share them.

learn: The American flag has 50 stars and 13 stripes. Its colours are red, white and blue.
The bald eagle is the national bird.
The Liberty Bell and the Statue of Liberty stand for freedom.
check: How many stripes are on the flag?
What do the Liberty Bell and the Statue of Liberty stand for?
lessons.try: Draw the flag and count the stripes as you draw.

learn: A monument is built to remember a person or event.
The Washington Monument honours George Washington, the first president.
Mount Rushmore has the faces of four presidents carved in stone.
check: Something built to remember a person or event
How many faces are on Mount Rushmore?
lessons.try: Look at a picture of Mount Rushmore and count the faces.

learn: Independence Day, July 4, celebrates when the country declared its independence in 1776.
Thanksgiving is a day to give thanks. Veterans Day honours people who served in the military.
Presidents' Day honours presidents. Martin Luther King Jr. Day honours a leader who worked for fairness.
check: People who served in the military
Martin Luther King Jr. worked for...
lessons.try: Pick a holiday and tell why it is celebrated.

learn: The flag has 13 stripes for the first colonies and 50 stars for the states.
Red stands for courage, white for purity and blue for justice.
People fly the flag on holidays and at schools.
check: Blue on the flag stands for...
lessons.try: Draw the flag and color it carefully.

learn: The bald eagle became our national bird in 1782.
It stands for strength and freedom.
It appears on coins and the Great Seal.
check: The bald eagle is our national...
lessons.try: Find the eagle on the back of a quarter.

learn: The Statue of Liberty is a symbol of freedom and welcome.
She was a gift from France in 1886.
Millions of immigrants saw her as they arrived in New York.
check: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from...
lessons.try: Make a crown like the Statue of Liberty's.

learn: The Liberty Bell rang in Philadelphia long ago.
It has a big crack and no longer rings.
It stands for freedom.
check: Does the Liberty Bell still ring?
lessons.try: Draw the Liberty Bell with its crack.

lessons.t: The White House and the Capitol
learn: The White House is where the president lives and works.
The Capitol is where Congress makes laws.
Both are in Washington, D.C.
lessons.try: Draw the White House and the Capitol dome.

learn: Monuments honor important people or events.
The Washington Monument is a tall stone tower. The Lincoln Memorial has a giant statue of Lincoln.
Mount Rushmore has four presidents carved in stone.
check: The Lincoln Memorial has a giant...
lessons.try: Design a monument for someone you admire.

learn: On July 4, 1776, America declared independence from Britain.
The Declaration of Independence said all people have rights.
We celebrate with fireworks, parades and picnics.
check: The Declaration of Independence said people have...
lessons.try: Make a Fourth of July poster.

learn: Presidents' Day is in February.
It honors George Washington and Abraham Lincoln, who were both born in February.
It also honors all presidents.

learn: Memorial Day in May remembers soldiers who died for our country.
Veterans Day in November thanks all who served in the military.
People visit cemeteries, march in parades and fly flags.

learn: Thanksgiving is in November.
It remembers the harvest feast of the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag in 1621.
Families gather to give thanks.
check: The 1621 feast was shared by Pilgrims and the...
lessons.try: Make a thankful list with your family.

learn: Dr. King's day is in January.
He worked peacefully so all people would have equal rights.
Many people do service projects on his day.
check: Dr. King worked ___ for equal rights.

lessons.try: Do a service project on MLK Day.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Symbols and Holidays
learn: The flag, bald eagle, Statue of Liberty and Liberty Bell are American symbols.
Monuments honor important people.
National holidays honor our history and heroes.
check: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from...
